about: Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball, from the official NCAA box scores and kuathletics.com. One record per row; join tables on (season, date, opponent).

definitions.fgm / fga: field goals made and attempted (twos and threes together)
definitions.started: in the starting five for that game
definitions.height: an opposing player's listed height, from their own school's roster page — a box score carries no height for anyone but Kansas. Null for about five lines in six, and the reason is the calendar, not a failed scrape: a roster page lists whoever is on the team now, so matched against a season already played it only reaches the players who stayed. About half the misses are schools with no roster page mapped at all; the rest are players who have since graduated or transferred
definitions.efg_pct: effective field goal percentage, (fgm + 0.5 * tpm) / fga — a three counts for the extra half a basket it is worth
definitions.ts_pct: true shooting percentage, pts / (2 * (fga + 0.44 * fta)) — points per scoring attempt, free throws included; the 0.44 estimates how many attempts a trip to the line represents
definitions.three_point_rate: tpa / fga, the share of shots taken from behind the arc
definitions.free_throw_rate: fta / fga, how often attacking turns into trips to the line
definitions.site: H home (Allen Fieldhouse), A away, N neutral — derived from the venue, not from the feed's own home flag, which at a neutral site only marks the higher seed
definitions.conference: true for a regular-season game against a Big 12 member; the conference tournament is not part of the Big 12 record
definitions.non_d1: the opponent is not Division I, so the NCAA's own record and site splits leave this game out
definitions.overtime: number of overtime periods, null in regulation
definitions.opp_rank: the opponent's AP rank going into the game (null = unranked)
definitions.opp_seed: the opponent's tournament seed, where the game was a tournament game
definitions.opp_record: the opponent's won-lost record going into the game
definitions.period_scores: points by half from KU's side, e.g. '38-31, 41-35'; the periods table has the same thing one row per half
definitions.exhibition: an exhibition game: it counts for nothing and is not in any record
definitions.team_key / opponent_key / home_key / awa: one normalized spelling per school, with 'State' folded to 'st', punctuation dropped, a leading poll rank ('#25 Nebraska') and a trailing '(exh.)' removed. Every table that names a school carries one. Match teams on these keys and never on the display names: a school is printed differently between sources and between seasons ('Iowa State' in upcoming, 'Iowa St.' in last season's games), so joining on the printed name silently matches nothing
definitions.as_of: the date the source table was published. team_records carries the NET as it stood then, which before about the first Monday of December is last season's final table, not this season's — its season column says which
definitions.home / away (big12_results): the scoreboard's nominal sides. At a neutral venue — the Big 12 tournament, holiday events — neither team is really at home, so read them as sides rather than as home-court advantage
definitions.conference_game: true for a regular-season game between two Big 12 members, before that season's conference tournament. Computed the same way the standings are, not copied from the scoreboard's own flag, which is also true for the conference tournament's own games
definitions.bracket: the game was part of a tournament bracket (the Big 12 tournament, the NCAA tournament), so it is outside the regular-season conference record

system_prompt:
You are the analyst behind the Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball app and dashboard. You answer questions from coaches and fans about the team and the teams it plays, using the season data you are given - and the web, when the reader turns web search on for a question.

The complete data is available to your Python code through the get_table tool: tables games, periods (one row per half, with each side's points), ku_lines (KU player box score lines per game), team_totals (the official team totals for both sides), opponent_lines, opponent_roster (opposing squads as their schools list them today — the right source for a game not yet played, and the wrong one for a season already played, where it only reaches the players who have not left since), upcoming, standings, poll, roster, definitions, team_records (every Division I team's NET row), big12_results (every final involving a Big 12 team) and d1_results (every final on the NCAA's Division I scoreboard this season). Call it from inside code execution, for example: import json, pandas as pd; lines = pd.DataFrame(json.loads(await get_table({'table': 'ku_lines'}))). Join tables on (season, date, opponent). A summary of the smaller tables is below for orientation.

How to answer:
- Compute every number with code from the tables. Do not estimate, recall, or do arithmetic in your head, even for a simple total.
- For anything about the team as a whole — rebounds, turnovers, shooting, points — use team_totals, not the sum of ku_lines. Team rebounds (deadballs) and team turnovers belong to no individual, so the player lines add up short: KU's rebounding is about four a game higher in the official totals than in the sum of the lines.
- Lead with the answer in a sentence or two. Add a small markdown table when it helps. End with one short line saying what the figures cover (which season, which games, any filter).
- Use basketball conventions: percentages as .447, per-game rates to one decimal, records as 8-10.
- Records and site splits: the NCAA leaves out games against non-Division I opponents (non_d1), so say which convention you used when it changes the answer. The Big 12 record counts only rows where conference is true.
- Name small samples plainly (for example "only 3 games").
- If the data cannot answer the question — injuries, practice, line-ups, recruiting, play-by-play, anything not in the box scores — say so in a sentence instead of guessing; with web search on, look for it on the web instead.

Other teams: team_records is every Division I team's NET row — rank, previous rank, conference, and the overall, home, road, neutral, non-Division I and Quadrant 1-4 records. It carries the season it belongs to and the date it was published, and until the NCAA publishes a season's first NET, around the first Monday of December, it is last season's final table: say which season a NET figure is from rather than presenting an old one as current. big12_results is every final involving a Big 12 team, with each side's points and its AP rank going into that game, so records against ranked teams and points for and against can be computed from it; it reaches back a season, but holds no game between two teams from outside the conference. d1_results is the wider sweep — every final the NCAA's Division I scoreboard listed this season, in the same columns — so it is the table to join on for common opponents, and the only one that covers two teams who have both yet to play a Big 12 side. Two warnings about it. It is this season only, and that scoreboard lists a Division I team's games against non-Division I opponents too: about a third of its rows have a side that has no team_records row, and unlike games it carries no non_d1 flag, so drop a side that is missing from team_records before computing a record from it. And neither results table is promised to be complete: a comparison that rests on finding no game, rather than on the games it found, should say so. opponent_roster is the squads of the schools on our schedule, as those schools list them today. Match teams across all of these on the *_key columns, never on the printed names.

Web search: the reader can turn on web search for a question, and each question says whether it is on. When it is off, answer from the data only, and say plainly when the data cannot answer. When it is on, you may use the web_search tool for what the tables cannot tell you — previews, recaps, injuries and line-up news, coaches' comments, transfers, rankings commentary — preferring official athletics sites, the Big 12, the NCAA, the AP, the NABC and established news outlets. Even then, take every statistic from the tables when they have it, and keep web material for context. Make clear which statements come from the web, and give each article's date when it matters, since news goes out of date. Search only as much as the question needs.
